overview: The Marshall Islands is a country of coral atolls and islands in the North Pacific. Its capital is Majuro. Run by the United States after the Second World War, it became independent in 1986 and keeps close ties with the US. In the 1940s and 1950s the United States tested nuclear weapons at Bikini and Enewetak atolls.

geography.text: The country is made up of 29 atolls and 5 single islands, arranged in two roughly parallel chains. The land is low and flat, mostly only a few metres above sea level, and Kwajalein atoll encloses one of the largest lagoons in the world.

subsections.title: Climate
subsections.text: Hot and humid, with a risk of typhoons.

subsections.title: Wildlife
subsections.text: Coral reefs full of fish and sharks.

history.text: Marshallese navigators crossed the open ocean using stick charts that mapped the patterns of waves. The islands were claimed by Germany and then Japan, and were captured by the United States in the Second World War. Between 1946 and 1958 the US tested 67 nuclear weapons at Bikini and Enewetak. The Marshall Islands became independent in 1986, in free association with the United States.

events.title: Japanese rule
events.text: Japan takes the islands during the First World War.

events.title: US capture
events.text: US forces take the islands from Japan.

events.title: Castle Bravo
events.text: The largest US nuclear test contaminates nearby islands.

government.text: The Marshall Islands is a republic with a mixed system: the parliament, the Nitijela, elects the President, who is both head of state and head of government. Under a Compact of Free Association, the United States provides defence and funding.

economy.text: The economy depends on US aid, fishing licences and a large international ship register, one of the biggest in the world. Many Marshallese have moved to the United States, which they can enter freely.

culture.text: Marshallese navigators used stick charts made of palm ribs and shells to map ocean swells. The islands are among the lowest-lying in the world. The legacy of US nuclear testing at Bikini and Enewetak, between 1946 and 1958, still affects communities today.

subsections.title: Traditions and festivals
subsections.text: A child's first birthday, kemem, is a big celebration.

sport.text: Basketball, volleyball and softball are popular, along with canoe racing in traditional outrigger canoes.

items.title: Outrigger canoes
items.text: Canoe races keep traditional boat-building alive.

didYouKnow: The bikini swimsuit was named after Bikini Atoll in 1946.
The Marshall Islands is one of the lowest-lying countries on Earth.
